Content projection: a reusable card component

ControlValueAccessor is the bridge between the forms API and any custom widget: writeValue pushes the model value into the view, and the registered onChange/onTouched callbacks report user changes back, which makes validators, dirty/touched and disable() work exactly as with a native input. Register it with the NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR multi-provider. Don't call onChange inside writeValue, or programmatic updates mark the form dirty.
Async validator: check that a username is available

Async validators run only after all sync validators pass, and the control's status is PENDING while they run. Angular unsubscribes from the previous validator observable when the value changes, so timer(400) plus switchMap acts as a debounce. The observable must complete (HTTP calls do); a never-ending stream such as valueChanges would leave the control pending forever.
Lazy-load a heavy component with @defer

Standalone components, directives and pipes used only inside a @defer block are split into a separate JavaScript chunk and downloaded when the trigger fires (on idle is the default; others are viewport, interaction, hover, timer(2s), immediate, or when a condition becomes true). It shrinks the initial bundle without any router changes. If the component is also used outside the block, it can't be deferred.
Unit test a service with HttpTestingController

provideHttpClientTesting() replaces the real backend, so no network calls happen. expectOne asserts exactly one matching request was made, flush supplies the response (or an error status), and verify() catches unexpected extra requests. Register provideHttpClient() first, then the testing provider. Interceptors can be tested the same way by adding withInterceptors([...]).
Component test with TestBed: set a signal input, click, assert the output

Standalone components need no declarations; TestBed.createComponent is enough (add imports/providers only for overrides). Use componentRef.setInput rather than assigning the property, because signal inputs are read-only. Query the DOM and assert what the user sees, not private fields. On Angular versions before linkedSignal, use a signal initialised in ngOnInit.
Reload data whenever a signal changes (toObservable + switchMap, or resource)

toObservable turns the input signal into a stream, switchMap cancels the previous request when the id changes (no race where an old response overwrites a new one), and toSignal converts back and unsubscribes automatically when the component is destroyed. Don't fetch inside effect(): effects are for side effects such as logging or syncing to localStorage, not for deriving state. The resource/rxResource APIs package this pattern with loading and error signals; their option names changed between versions, so describe them generically if unsure.
Infinite scroll directive with IntersectionObserver

An IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element is far cheaper than listening to every scroll event. The loading flag prevents duplicate requests while one is in flight, and the sentinel is removed when there is no more data. For very long lists, add virtual scrolling (CDK cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport) so only visible rows are rendered.
Two-way binding with model() and signal queries with viewChild()

model() creates a writable signal input; calling set inside the child emits checkedChange, so the parent's banana-in-a-box [(checked)] stays in sync, and it can bind directly to a parent signal. viewChild(), viewChildren() and contentChild() return signals, so there is no need to wait for ngAfterViewInit and they work in computed. Use .required when the element always exists.
switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap

| switchMap | mergeMap | concatMap | exhaustMap
New value while inner is running | Cancels the old inner | Runs both at once | Queues it, runs after | Ignores the new value
Order of results | Only the latest | Whichever finishes first | Same as input | Only the first
Typical use | Typeahead, route param → load | Independent parallel requests | Saves that must stay in order | Login / submit button double clicks
Risk | Cancelling a write you needed | Too many parallel calls | Slow queue builds up | Losing clicks you wanted
Rule of thumb: reads that only care about the latest → switchMap; writes → concatMap (or exhaustMap for a submit button); mergeMap when order and cancellation do not matter.
Subject vs BehaviorSubject vs ReplaySubject

| Subject | BehaviorSubject | ReplaySubject(n)
Initial value | None | Required | None
Late subscriber gets | Only future values | Latest value at once, then future | Last n values, then future
Read current value synchronously | No | Yes, .value | No
Typical use | Events: "saved", "logout clicked" | State: current user, cart | Cache of recent messages
Rule of thumb: events → Subject, state → BehaviorSubject. In Angular 17+ new component and service state is usually a signal, which also always has a current value.
Reactive forms vs template-driven forms

| Reactive (FormGroup, FormControl) | Template-driven (ngModel)
Form model lives in | Component class | Template, created by directives
Typing | Strongly typed since Angular 14 | Looser
Dynamic fields | Easy with FormArray | Awkward
Custom and cross-field validators | Plain functions | Need a directive
Unit testing | Test the class, no DOM needed | Needs the template rendered
Good for | Most business forms | Tiny forms: a search box, a toggle
Rule of thumb: reactive forms for anything with validation rules or dynamic sections (a patient intake form); template-driven only when the form is one or two simple fields.
Default vs OnPush change detection

| Default | OnPush
Component is checked | On every change-detection run | Only when marked dirty
Marked dirty by | n/a | New input reference, a DOM event in it or its children, async pipe emission, a signal read in its template changing, markForCheck()
Mutating an input object | Shows up | Not seen (same reference)
Cost on big pages | Grows with the whole tree | Skips untouched subtrees
Rule of thumb: use OnPush everywhere with signals or immutable inputs. If a view "does not update", look for code that mutates an object or array instead of replacing it.
Signal vs Observable: which do you use for what?

| signal / computed | Observable (RxJS)
Always has a value | Yes, read with count() | No; may emit zero, one or many values
Push or pull | Change pushes "dirty", readers pull the value | Pushes values to subscribers
Subscriptions to clean up | None | Yes (async pipe, takeUntilDestroyed)
Time and async operators | No (debounce, retry, cancel need RxJS) | Yes: debounceTime, switchMap, retry
Best for | UI state and derived values | Events over time, HTTP, WebSockets
Rule of thumb: keep streams in RxJS and state in signals; bridge them with toSignal() and toObservable() from @angular/core/rxjs-interop.
